raw_response:
Well, I've been at this for fifty years now on the same ground, so you could say I don't think too hard about most of it — I just do what works. My wife and I are the only ones left at home; the kids are in the city and send some money, but the 14 mu of land is still mine to manage. At my age I can't do heavy work like I used to, so I hire the combine and the planter when the neighbors do — we all split the cost and the machine comes around.

For the wheat I'll plant around mid-October like always, right after the rain if there's one. I buy seed from the supply station — an improved variety, the one most people around here use. For fertilizer I don't measure it out like the young agricultural college types do. I buy two bags of compound fertilizer per mu before planting — that's the 15-15-15 stuff, about 50 jin a bag — and then when the wheat turns green in spring and starts standing up at jointing, I top-dress with urea, maybe 30 jin per mu. If the wheat looks a bit yellow I'll add a little more; if it looks dark green I'll hold back. That's how my father did it and it's how I do it.

I irrigate the wheat three times — once before winter so the roots take hold, once at jointing in spring, and once when the grain is filling out. The well is shared in our village and each round costs real money, so I don't do more unless it's a dry year. Last year we got maybe 420 kg per mu, which is about normal. The neighbors around me get similar.

For the maize, as soon as the wheat is off the field in June I have the custom planter come the same week — you can't wait, the season is too short. I use hybrid seed, the kind the seed shop pushes. For fertilizer I put down one bag of compound when planting and then top-dress urea at the big-trumpet stage, about 25 jin per mu. Maize doesn't need as much water as wheat if the summer rains come — some years I don't irrigate at all, some years once or twice if July is dry. I plan for one irrigation and see what the sky does.

Pesticide — I spray herbicide on the wheat in spring for the weeds, and on the maize when it's small. For bugs, only if I see them. I don't spray just in case, it costs too much.

I keep some cash back for emergencies. Two old people, you never know. I don't try to squeeze the last kilogram out of the land — I just want a steady year like the last one.
